title: Micro-surge impedance scratchpad
content:
Notes to self - running a small battery of micro-surge (very short, high qps bursts) experiments to characterize an "impedance" phenomenon: bursts that should fit in capacity still see p99 blow-ups unless certain layers warm up or cache/kv paths align.

Overview:
- Goal: understand why short 2–6s surges at 150–400 qps create p99 latency spikes even when average load is low and GPU occupancy is moderate.
- Hypothesis: mismatch between request batching window, KV cache priming, and scheduler slices (time-sliced preemption). Also possible GC/worker spinup on the worker side.

Setup:
- Model: opt-6.7b-quantized (int8-ish config from PR #2107)
- Fleet: 4x A10G (dedicated pool), runtime version: canary-2024-11-01
- Client: custom load-replay tool (node) that sends Poisson bursts with tight windows
- Batching policy: adaptive, target latency 120ms, max batch 64
- KV cache enabled: LRU, per-worker shard, 128MB each

Commands (repro):
- run replay: ./replay --pattern microburst --qps 300 --duration 4 --clients 60 --payload small
- profiling: RB: curl -sS http://metrics/point?range=1m | jq .latency_hist

Raw quick results (aggregate from 5 runs):
- baseline (no cache priming): qps 300, p50=24ms, p95=94ms, p99=1.28s, error=0.4%
- primed-kv (run lightweight priming sequence 5s before burst): qps 300, p50=22ms, p95=68ms, p99=128ms, error=0.02%
- reduced-batch-window (target 60ms): qps 300, p50=26ms, p95=72ms, p99=266ms, error=0.1%
- disable-preempt (scheduler hint no-preempt for 8s): qps 300, p50=23ms, p95=64ms, p99=142ms

Observations / notes:
- The huge p99 in baseline aligns with first 1.5s of burst; telemetry shows many requests miss KV cache and cause decoder/infer cold path plus slight queueing.
- Priming sequence (cheap empty-context warmups) drastically reduces p99. Suggests prefix/KV cache + operator kernel memory path is dominant.
- Reducing batch window helped p95 but p99 still high unless cache primed. Means batching alone is insufficient for micro-surges.
- Scheduler preemption correlated with spike tail; disabling preempt reduces—but does not eliminate—spike. Might be worker hotpath blocked by GC or wakeups.

Hypotheses to test next:
1) Batch + cache coordination: ensure priming requests also insert kv shards across all workers (shard-uniform priming).
2) Background GC/alloc: run heap-prof and reduce allocations during priming to see effect.
3) Network / NLB cold path: check conn-reuse and TLS session resumption counts during first second.
4) Client-side pacing: test many small clients vs fewer large to see fanout effects.

Quick follow-ups (TODO):
- [ ] Add a controlled priming task into rollout canary for 60s after deploy and measure micro-surge resilience (ticket INF-5237)
- [ ] Add metric: kv_miss_rate_by_worker (already instrumented? verify)
- [ ] Run same runs with quantized vs fp16 to see kernel selection overheads
- [ ] Schedule a 30m sync with Ishaan + Olivia to align experiments (slot: Mon 10:00)
mini_summary: Scratchpad for micro-surge impedance effect; priming KV/cache reduces p99 dramatically — batching settings help p95 but not p99 unless cache is primed. Next: coordinate priming + test GC and kernel overheads.
